articles.title_orig: Stock futures fall on speculation Democrats to win big in midterms, slow data center buildout: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures fall on speculation Democrats to win big in midterms, slow data center buildout: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures dropped on Tuesday evening as traders speculated that Democrats were headed for majority control of Congress and some key gubernatorial wins in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections .
Futures tied to the S&P 500 traded 1.3% lower, while Nasdaq-100 futures shed 2.2%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 410 points, or 0.8%.
Kalshi odds for Democratic Senate control increased to above 99%, showing traders were increasingly betting on a big night for Democrats. Odds for Democratic control of the House, which was largely expected, jumped to 99% for Democrats. CNBC's Election Desk projects that Democrats will win the U.S. House. Democrats are also pacing to gain control of the Senate.
Republican incumbent Greg Abbott has called Texas Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa to concede, according to MS Now. Hinojosa has pledged a moratorium on data centers in the key tech hub.
If Democrats are able to secure a sizable majority in the Senate — the so-called blue wave scenario —  the market and especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence buildout could come under pressure , according to some on Wall Street. Investors fear a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. AI-linked stocks have already pulled back in recent weeks on concern about a slowing pace in data-center spending.
Big Tech shares Microsoft , Amazon and Nvidia were all trading lower in extended trading. High-risk data center play CoreWeave was down 6% in Robinhood overnight trading. Elon Musk's SpaceX was also off by 6% on Robinhood.
Equities "trended lower as it's looked more likely that Democrats are going to pick up the House and most likely the Senate," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial.
"I think it'll be more interesting on how the governorships go," Saglimbene added. "If you get some governorships that are Democratic, what does that mean for the data center buildout, which has already seen a lot of skepticism over the last couple weeks in terms of the hyperscaler capex spending."
To be sure, the polls have yet to fully close in all states. Election nights have often shown wild swings in markets. Many investors also believe any market move from this election would be short lived.
AMD shares initially surged double digits in post-market action after the company, a key player in the AI trade, reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations. The stock was last up about 3% higher as stock market futures gave up their gains.
On the overall market, investors believe a blue wave would also be a headwind as it likely rules out any more business-friendly policies like tax breaks and possibly increases scrutiny on industries like banking.
Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3.5% in Robinhood trading.
As equity futures fell into the red, Treasury yields moved lower, with the 10-year Treasury note yield dropping more than 4 basis points to 4.904%. Futures on the Cboe Volatility Index fear gauge increased, rising above 20 , as investors braced for a pullback.
Shares of Trump Media & Technology declined more than 7% in overnight trading on Robinhood as the 2026 midterm elections appear poised to conclude with a blue wave.
The stock moved lower after CNBC's Election Desk projected that Democrats are going to win the House. The party was also on track to take Senate control from Republicans.
President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post late Tuesday, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"
Treasury yields fell as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped nearly 5 basis points to 4.902%. The 30-year bond yield slid 5.29%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 6 basis points to 4.55%. Read more .
Shares of SpaceX fell more than 6% on Robinhood overnight trading as Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa continued her lead over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the Texas gubernatorial race.
"Let's watch SpaceX. Let's watch Tesla . This is Elon Musk-land now. There are a lot of California companies that moved to Texas, thinking, 'All right, we're going to get out of this blue state and go somewhere safe,' and now it's proven that it isn't," Jay Woods, Freedom Capital Markets' chief market strategist, said in an interview with CNBC.
"You want to watch a lot of these Texas companies that moved there," he stressed.
Musk said that he was going to move the headquarters of both companies to Texas from California back in 2024. Tesla shares were down more than 4% on Robinhood.
Investors were focusing on the results of the Texas gubernatorial race for clues about the AI trade because the state represents an outsized portion of data center capacity. Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa has an early lead over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Hinojosa is calling for an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state and an end any tax incentives for the build-out.
"The one thing that could really end up moving stuff though would be if Abbott were to lose Texas," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer of Horizon Investments. "Because there is a legitimate question about, where do you build these data centers?"
"Texas is a fertile ground for that. And if he were to lose, I think that fertile ground is largely barren. So, that's going to be a challenge. And so the AI trade — at least for next couple days — does hinge on does Abbott win or not," Ladner added.
Texas represents about 27% of U.S. data center gigawatts, estimates Wells Fargo.
— John Melloy and Sarah Min
Any big surprises out of the 2026 midterm elections could mean buying opportunities for investors, according to Angelo Kourkafas, senior strategist at Edward Jones.
"The results could act as a clearing event removing some uncertainty, though developments around the AI theme and geopolitics are the primary forces driving markets heading into the final two months of the year," he said.
However, he added: "If we do see election-driven volatility it may present an opportunity for long-term investors to lean into it."
HSBC said on Wednesday it had issued $4.25 billion in senior unsecured debt in two tranches, including $1.75 billion in notes due in 2032 at 5.819% fixed-rate/floating-rate and another $2.5 billion in notes maturing in 2037 at 6.262%.
Europe's largest bank, which plans to list the securities on the New York Stock Exchange, did not specify how the funds raised would be deployed.
Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) futures moved higher on Tuesday evening as U.S. equity futures came under pressure amid results from the midterm elections.
Futures tied to the VIX, otherwise referred to as Wall Street's " fear gauge ," were last seen trading at 20.90.
A move above 20 tends to be a key level signaling heightened angst among investors in the market.
Investors are on edge as polls across the U.S. begin closing in an election that could bring gridlock to government. But if history is any indication, they may have little to worry about.
A CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024 shows the benchmark rose an average of 0.2% one day after the election and 1.1% in the month following. One year out, the benchmark averages a 13.8% return and rose in 91% of cases. That's including general elections.
Looking at just post-midterm returns, the record is even stronger. The S&P 500 has risen after each of the last 11 midterm elections between 1982 and 2022. One year out, the index returns 13.7% on average.
Read the full story here .
— Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells
The Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) rose by 1.3% in after hours trading on

articles.title_orig: Flights across Europe searched and diverted after hoax bomb threats
articles.title_zh: Flights across Europe searched and diverted after hoax bomb threats
articles.content_orig:
Unclear if series of incidents affecting two UK departures and several Ryanair services, among others, were connected
Seven planes across Europe have been searched or diverted after a series of bomb threats were made to passenger flights, prompting questions as to whether there was any coordination behind the warnings.
Two UK departures – one from Heathrow and one from Manchester – were among those threatened in what Downing Street called “malicious hoaxes”, though all planes landed safely and no explosives were found.
A UK Department for Transport source added that the low-level threats were “not credible” and that passengers should not be concerned, though the warnings disrupted flights and prompted investigations across the UK and Europe.
None of the incidents and subsequent searches threw up any evidence of terrorist activity, though authorities were responding to an unusual number of reported threats in one day.
One of Warsaw’s two main airports, Modlin, was briefly closed after receiving a diverted plane, and Polish officials confirmed that they had received bomb threats involving two flights coming into the capital.
Italian fighter jets escorted a Ryanair plane into Rome following a warning of a suspected threat on a flight coming from Dublin. The flight landed safely and nothing untoward was reported as being found.
There was little obvious pattern surrounding the incidents, which affected flights taking off from the UK, Ireland, Denmark, Portugal and Italy, and landing in Poland, Spain, Italy and Bulgaria . Four of the flights were operated by Ryanair, the others by Wizz Air, LOT and SAS.
Investigators added there was no immediate evidence of a hostile state being behind the threats, though they continued to monitor developments, sharing information across the continent while inquiries continued.
Aviation security fears have been reignited with the recent FlyDubai incident when a co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash a Tel Aviv-bound plane. Russia has also been accused of being behind firebomb threats targeting parcel carriers using cargo planes over the past two years.
The threats followed an incident on Monday when another flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted, apparently without substance.
Experts said that fake threats occur on a daily basis. Philip Baum, visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, said: “Most are from individuals who think it is funny or want to delay a flight for some reason. If the industry was to respond to every unsubstantiated threat, flights would grind to a halt.
“The reality is that terrorist organisations who might like to smuggle a bomb on to a flight don’t tell people, they claim responsibility after the attacks.”
But he added that the fact that some aircraft did divert would “imply that the threats are credible and specific in nature, and therefore one has to respond accordingly”.
Tuesday’s series of incidents started with a flight from Heathrow operated by the Polish carrier LOT, which was scheduled to arrive at Warsaw’s Chopin airport but was diverted to the second airport, further from the Polish capital, Modlin. Authorities closed that airport after the alert and the Boeing 737 Max landed without incident.
“The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found,” spokesperson Adam Szablowski told AFP. “The airport has been reopened and is operating normally.”
A Scandinavian Airlines plane from Copenhagen to Warsaw was also the subject of a threat but landed at Chopin airport, where a security inspection that did not turn up any explosive devices closed part of the airport.
Another UK departure, a Ryanair plane from Manchester, was met by emergency vehicles on landing at its destination, Murcia in southern Spain , after another threat. Spanish regional authorities confirmed on social media that no explosives were found on the flight.
The Metropolitan police confirmed its aviation unit is monitoring the situation, adding no security issues were identified following threats made against flights after they had taken off.
A UK government spokesperson said of the threats to two departures from Britain: “The UK has one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we’ve seen today.
“Our world-leading police and intelligence agencies work closely every day to keep us safe, using the tools they have to assess and respond to potential threats.”
In Italy, two Ryanair flights were searched at Rome’s Fiumicino airport following potential bomb threats, according to the airport operator ADR. The first was a flight from Lisbon, while a second later in the morning from Dublin was escorted in by Italian air force fighter jets until landing.
Bulgaria’s ​transport ‌ministry said ‌in a statement to ‌Reuters that threats were ​made against a Wizz Air flight ⁠from Bergamo and a Ryanair flight from Dublin to ⁠the capital, Sofia. Both flights were carrying about 180 passengers and landed safely, with no devices found.
The separate incidents came the day after a Wizz Air service from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet.
The plane, which was due to depart from Luton at 8.15am on Monday for Sofia, was diverted after a bomb threat was received “during the flight”, Wizz Air said.
Airlines abide by a regulated process to assess and manage bomb threats, although virtually all are fake. In the UK, airlines file a mandatory occurrence report to the Civil Aviation Authority .
Ryanair did not respond to requests for comment.

Lin believes that divorce does not mean becoming strangers, emphasising her deep desire to repay the kindness she once received
A woman from central China has moved many online after inviting her ex-mother-in-law to live with her following the deaths of her ex-husband and ex-father-in-law.
Lin, from Henan province, recently flew more than 1,000km to Guangdong province in southern China to bring her ex-mother-in-law to live with her, despite having divorced her ex-husband 12 years ago.
Lin made the decision after her ex-father-in-law died of an illness in 2024 and her ex-husband died last year.

articles.title_orig: How malware and a bogus job interview let attackers nab $6.3B from Binance
articles.title_zh: How malware and a bogus job interview let attackers nab $6.3B from Binance
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Hackers behind the record-breaking Binance heist spent weeks masquerading as recruiters and fake executives, eventually convincing an engineer to download malicious software onto a work computer as part of a larger-scale ruse, the company said Tuesday.
Binance said the ploy included two rounds of interviews, with a supposed human resources representative conducting the first interview and sharing social media information to gain the programmer's trust. A second person, posing as the CEO of a fake company, later persuaded the engineer to download a file containing malware under the guise of an interview assessment.
"This was a complex attack," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on social media Monday. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."
The company emphasized that there was no single breach or mistake behind the hack, which is by far the largest crypto theft in history . Instead, the campaign unfolded over several months.
Here's what you need to know:
The fake job interview was just one stage of the hackers' multistep attack. Binance said the campaign began in June, when another engineer downloaded a "popular AI coding tool." Additional employee devices were later compromised before the hackers gained access to systems involved in authorizing wallet transactions.
On Oct. 20, hackers used the engineer's laptop, which had been compromised during the fake interview process, to infiltrate two other employees' computers. Binance said the attackers also used an internal AI tool, though it did not provide further details on how the tool was used. Days later, they used stolen credentials to launch the malware responsible for the unauthorized transfers.
Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but a broader review revealed a wider series of security breaches. The company temporarily suspended withdrawals late last week before reopening them Sunday.
Hours after the hack, Binance said it would cover all customer losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users . Stablecoin issuers including Tether and Circle ( CRCL ) were able to freeze a little less than half of the stolen assets.
By late Sunday night ET, the company said it had processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and roughly $1.01 billion in deposits. Binance says it has since replenished 98% of the affected assets.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance in an interview that aired Tuesday morning . "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the system's back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss."
Binance attributed the attack to North Korea, following a similar finding by the Federal Bureau of Investigation over the weekend and by outside investigators. North Korea denied the allegations Monday.
Binance added that it has fended off 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats so far this year.
Follow David Hollerith on X @DsHollers .

articles.title_orig: Canva Announces Layoffs, Job Changes for About 22% of Workforce
articles.title_zh: Canva Announces Layoffs, Job Changes for About 22% of Workforce
articles.content_orig:
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

articles.title_orig: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.title_zh: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.content_orig:
Workers inside Google’s artificial-intelligence division are asking executives to release them from non-disparagement agreements so they can discuss AI’s risks in public, The Washington Post reported. The request puts a plain question in front of one of the world’s most powerful AI employers: who gets to speak when the people closest to the technology think the public deserves a warning?
The reported dispute involves employees at Google DeepMind, including staff in London. A contract reviewed by The Washington Post reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, including after they leave Google. Two current Google DeepMind workers told the paper that the agreements restrict public communication about AI’s potential impacts.
Google has pushed back on part of the picture. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A Google spokesperson added that the company does not enforce such clauses after employees leave and provides internal channels for escalating concerns. Disclosure pressure on AI labs is rising on several fronts, and our look at what the Anthropic amended S-1 disclosed on November 2 shows how much a lab now has to tell investors. This story asks the mirror-image question: how much can its workers tell everyone else?
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Four points hold up in the reporting available to us. First, workers in Google’s AI division are asking executives for release from non-disparagement agreements. Second, the dispute concerns Google DeepMind staff, including people based in London. Third, a contract The Washington Post reviewed reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, even after they leave. Fourth, two current DeepMind workers said the agreements limit what they can say publicly about AI’s possible impacts.
Those are the load-bearing facts. Everything else around this story, including some of the headline phrasing that has circulated, goes further than the record does. The idea that Google researchers are collectively demanding the freedom to tell the world what they know about AI is a fair summary of the mood, but it is not independently established beyond the worker requests The Washington Post described. We have no verified count of participating researchers, no list of signatories, and no named organizer.
We also have no on-record quote from a named Google DeepMind researcher in the material available for this report. That matters for how much weight readers should put on any single claim. The two current workers appear in the reporting as sources describing the agreements, not as named spokespeople for a movement. A story built on a reviewed contract and two employees is still news, but it is a narrower story than a walkout or an open letter would be.
One detail deserves attention. The workers are reported to be asking executives to release them, which is a request, not a breach. That choice signals that at least some staff want to stay inside the rules while changing them. It also suggests they see the contract language, not company culture, as the obstacle.
A non-disparagement clause is a contract term that limits what a person can say publicly about their employer. Standard versions cover false or damaging statements. Broader versions can reach honest criticism, opinions, and even neutral descriptions of internal decisions if the wording is loose enough. Companies use them to protect reputation, and employees often sign them as part of an offer letter or a separation package without reading the fine print twice.
The difference between a narrow clause and a broad one is the whole story here. A narrow clause leaves room for a worker to say that a safety process failed or that a product carries a risk the public should weigh. A broad one makes the worker think twice before saying anything at all. When the subject is AI risk, a field where insiders often know things outsiders cannot check, that chilling effect carries real cost.
The reported contract goes beyond a standard employment-period restriction. According to The Washington Post, it bars some British employees from criticizing Google for life, including after they leave. A restriction that survives employment has no natural end date. A researcher who quits after five years of safety work would stay bound in year ten, even if the technology and the risks look nothing like they did at signing.
Note the qualifier in the reporting: the reviewed contract covers some British employees, not every DeepMind worker. We do not know the exact language used across the workforce, and the reporting does not claim a single uniform clause. Any reader judging Google’s conduct should keep that gap in view.
Google answered with two statements. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A spokesperson also said Google does not enforce non-disparagement clauses after employees leave, and that the company provides internal channels for people to escalate concerns.
Both statements carry weight, and both leave questions open. Removing the post-termination portion for new hires is a concrete contract change. It tells us Google’s lawyers saw enough risk or enough pressure to rewrite the template. A non-enforcement pledge is softer. It describes what the company does today, not what the paper allows tomorrow.
That distinction explains why employees are reported to be seeking clearer legal protection through revised contract language. A worker deciding whether to speak at a conference or give a journalist a background interview does not rely on a spokesperson’s description of enforcement habits. They rely on the text they signed. If the text says one thing and the practice says another, the safest move for the individual is silence.
Internal escalation channels address a different problem. They give employees a place to raise concerns inside the company, which helps when management listens. They do nothing for a worker who has raised concerns internally, seen no change, and now wants the public to know. The workers’ request, as reported, targets that second situation.
Google’s stated fix applies to new hires. The reporting we have does not say whether current employees, or people who already left under older terms, get the same change. That gap is the center of the dispute. A policy that improves the paperwork for the next cohort leaves the people who raised the issue on the old terms.
Several questions follow, and none has a confirmed answer in the available reporting:
Each question has a simple yes or no answer that Google could publish. The company’s decision on whether to answer them will say more about its posture than the original contract language did.
News about AI labs moves fast and headlines tend to outrun facts. The table below separates what the reporting supports from what it does not, so readers can see where the evidence stops.
Two lessons come out of that table. The core facts are solid because they rest on a document the paper reviewed and on company statements. The movement framing is softer, and readers should treat it as interpretation until someone names organizers or publishes a letter.
The reported contract covers British employees, and DeepMind has a major presence in London. That puts the dispute inside a country with its own regulators, its own employment rules, and its own public conversation about AI. UK officials have been vocal about AI risk in other domains. Our earlier report on the NCSC warning that AI malware could hit UK critical infrastructure within two years shows how seriously British security agencies treat the subject.
A government that asks the public to take AI risk seriously will find it awkward when the people who build the technology say they cannot

articles.title_zh: Midterm election results 2026: Who’s winning and what’s at stake for stocks and the economy
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Control of the US Congress is the prize on November 3, 2026, as Democrats attempt to wrest majorities from President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterm elections.
Voters will also choose governors in 36 of the 50 states, and nearly every state will hold elections for its state-level legislative bodies.
Ballots have been cast for weeks, with early voting underway across the country ahead of Election Day .
The midterms , held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, by definition do not involve the president himself.
But anyone tempted to dismiss this year's contests as lacking drama or importance should weigh two statistics.
More than 100 million people are expected to cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022.
And as of October 30, a record $11.6 billion had been spent on political advertisements for the 2025–26 election cycle.
AdImpact, which tracks the activities, said the top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan.
Campaign finance records show Elon Musk alone has spent $442 million to support Republicans.
Midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races.
For example, more than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election.
In the House, Republicans currently hold a 218-214 majority, with two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans.
Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.
The Senate is also in play, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority.
Democrats must net four additional seats to get control there.
Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.
Trump's approval of his performance is at an all-time low of 32 percent, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to affect the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.
Evidence suggests Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans.
If early voting trends continue, it could point to a Democratic win in November.
There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.
A landslide for the Democrats, however, is far from assured.
Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism toward Democrats, a Republican spending advantage in campaigns, and fears among moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.
Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress.
For 2026, that means Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.
The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.
Midterm election results can also give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.
Recent history shows the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.
In the 2010 midterms, during Barack Obama's Democratic presidency, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation.
Democrats lost their majority.
In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.
The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time.
He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.
Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House.
They gained a net 40 House seats but lost a net two Senate seats.
At the state level, Republicans currently control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.
If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
He is currently the House Democratic leader.
Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to investigate a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates.
Jeffries has repeatedly said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.
Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House.
He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.
A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job.
Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."
Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign.
An open seat in a Nebraska swing district, where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran, is also drawing attention.
Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.
Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.
Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence.
State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.
There is no set time for when the world will learn the results of the US midterm elections.
In tight races, winners may not be called for days or even weeks.
The first individual race calls are expected to start after polls begin to close in the United States on Tuesday night, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. (ET) (2300 GMT).
Polls then close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4).
The last polls to close are in far western Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Election Night: Dow Futures, AI Stocks, Elon Musk In Focus; AMD, Arista Lead Earnings Winners (Live)
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Election Night: Dow Futures, AI Stocks, Elon Musk In Focus; AMD, Arista Lead Earnings Winners (Live)
articles.content_orig:
Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading.
Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter:
Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement . Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results.
CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth.
"We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call.
AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand .
The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago.
After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October.
"Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts.
AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI.
AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple.
Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research .
AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago.
For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount.
AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering.
AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering .
During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung.
In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications.

articles.title_orig: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
articles.title_zh: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
articles.content_orig:
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. I’ll tell you what I tell them: If I knew that, I would make a life-changing bet on the market, levered up as far as I could, and then, after I made my money, go retire on a beach somewhere. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows.
What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “ Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks .” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.”
“What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The astronomically expensive AI buildout has swamped debt markets — making it harder to raise cash. But there’s still more debt coming, and people still want to buy it. For instance, Meta drew $58 billion in orders for a bond offering that’s expected to be $15 billion to $20 billion, Bloomberg reported today. Oracle said Monday it would need another $20 billion in bonds , on top of its existing steep commitments . Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is selling €6 billion (or about $6.7 billion) of bonds. Even Microsoft recently sold bonds , for the first time in a decade — $25 billion of them.
The PIMCO CEO — his name is Emmanuel Roman, but his job is what matters here — has estimated that the AI buildout could create $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years. The entire total US bond market is about $12 trillion.
I am harping on PIMCO because it has been instrumental in the AI trade. It was among the group of financiers that did the first CoreWeave chip-based financing in 2023. It made a quick $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds , meant to support the AI buildout, last year. It bought $4 billion of SpaceX bonds last month. If PIMCO’s CEO is publicly sounding the alarm about a bubble popping, that’s a big deal — especially since the company just sold a bunch of its AI debt .
It’s not just PIMCO urging caution. Apollo Global Management, which lately had been talking with SpaceX about a $40 billion chip deal , is also warning of AI risk. Apollo president Jim Zelter told analysts today that while he expects society will use “dramatically more computing power in the future” and that AI is improving quickly, there is still significant uncertainty. “What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The sheer volume of interest on Meta’s bonds suggests we are not at the top of the market. But there have been reports from China that its AI bubble burst some time ago. Meanwhile Wall Street banks were tripping over themselves to finance $63 billion in debt from Anthropic — not even a hyperscaler.
This is what I mean when I say “I don’t know.” I do think, though, that something major — PIMCO’s Roman singled out US rate hikes, war, or a eurozone crisis as potential triggers — could flip this market. We’re not in go-go-go territory now. Maybe that will change; it’s possible Anthropic’s IPO will go blockbuster and it’ll be like when someone rolls up to a party that’s running low on beer with a 24-pack. But as more people are expressing caution — and particularly after the disaster at Situational Awareness — the best part of the party might be over.

articles.title_orig: Chicago Voters Spend Hours In Line As Polling Places Run Out Of Ballots Across City
articles.title_zh: Chicago Voters Spend Hours In Line As Polling Places Run Out Of Ballots Across City
articles.content_orig:
CHICAGO — Residents across the city are enduring long wait times to vote as some polling places haven’t had enough paper ballots — with multiple locations running out of them twice on Tuesday.
Polling places ran out of paper ballots for Tuesday’s midterm election, including voting sites in Uptown, Pilsen, Logan Square, Albany Park and the Near West Side, voters and poll workers told Block Club.
In those cases, voters had to wait to use the few electronic voting booths that were available, leading to long lines and harsh words for election officials.
On the Far North Side, Goudy Elementary School, 5120 N. Winthrop Ave., ran out of paper ballots for some 48th Ward voters by 8:15 a.m. Tuesday, prompting a long wait to use the single electronic voting machine, election judge Adam Honaker said. The polling place was initially given 50 paper ballots, he said.
Neighbor Kerri Rackow said she got in line around 9:30 a.m. and was still waiting to use the electronic machine as of 11:45 a.m.
Honaker said he was told by election officials that additional ballots were being printed and sent over, but at noon, he still didn’t have a definitive timeline. Voters were being informed they could go to any of the citywide polling places to cast their vote instead.
The Board of Elections said Tuesday that it was investigating ballot shortages at multiple polling places Tuesday, with the problem appearing to be concentrated in precincts that use multiple ballot styles.
The board first heard reports of a shortage in the 1st Ward around 10 a.m. Tuesday and immediately began printing additional ballots at its Downtown warehouse to send to affected precincts, said Board of Elections interim spokesperson Julie Metea.
The board is focusing its investigation on so-called split precincts, where precinct boundaries are divided among different jurisdictions and voters can have several different ballot styles. Some of those precincts can have as many as seven ballot combinations, Metea said.
Metea told Block Club that the elections board is working to resolve the shortages and ensure voters can cast ballots, Metea said. Voters who encounter long lines or ballot shortages can go to one of the city’s universal voting sites, which are early voting centers equipped to accommodate larger crowds and move lines more quickly. However, a line of voters outside the Downtown supersite snaked down several city blocks.
“We apologize. It is frustrating, but we’re working the problem, investigating and accommodating voters,” Metea told Block Club.
She said the board received confirmed ballot shortage reports in Ward 1, Precinct 4, and that the board also is looking into similar reports in Ward 1, Precinct 5, as well as Wards 25 and 32.
Voters who are in line by 7 p.m. will be allowed to vote.
Metea also attributed a strong in-person turnout to Tuesday’s long lines as 232,672 ballots were cast at polling places as of 3:15 p.m. Tuesday. That compares with about 227,633 Election Day ballots cast by around the same time during the 2022 midterm election, according to Chicago Board of Elections figures.
Mike Nellis, the Democratic committeeman for the 32nd Ward, said Holstein Park ran out of paper ballots around 10 am. He said the polling place, which has one electronic machine, received 50 more ballots later that morning and was told they would be given more but never were.
As of 5 pm on Tuesday, Nellis said there was at least a two-hour wait to vote at Holstein Park.
“This is completely unacceptable and they should have been better prepared. They should have known there would be high voter turnout given the national climate and they should have know there would be some confusion around the school board,” Nellis said.
“People should not have to wait two hours to vote especially in a city as progressive as Chicago,” he said.
In Albany Park, resident Emily Hilleren tried to vote at Roosevelt High School, 3436 W. Wilson Ave., around 11:50 a.m. Tuesday and found that the line stretched out of the door to the sidewalk. She was told the polling place had run out of paper ballots and only had one electronic voting machine.
Hilleren and a few other voters decided to walk to the American Indian Center, one of the city-wide polling places, which is just a few blocks away, and voted there. She said the American Indian Center had a short line and nine electronic voting machines.
“I’ve been voting at Roosevelt since 2020 and this is the first time I’ve seen the line even out the door so the fact that it was all the way to the sidewalk was wild,” Hilleren said.
At 4:50 p.m., the line at Roosevelt High School stretched outside the front doors to the corner of Wilson and Kimball avenues.
“I’ve been doing this for 10 years and we’ve never had this,” said Kim Smolen, an election judge.
Smolen said the site ran out of paper ballots by 11:30 a.m. She said they were only given about 150 ballots for school board district 3A, but they were given 1,700 ballots for district 2B. The voting location only has one electronic machine, she said. Smolen, who had been at the location since 4:45 a.m. said judges received more paper ballots around 3 p.m.
Dan Doyen, an election judge at Noble Square Cooperative, 1165 N. Milwaukee Ave., said the polling place “almost immediately” ran out of paper ballots for some 27th Ward voters Tuesday morning, which forced people to wait to use the single electronic voting machine.
Doyen said the Board of Elections was contacted right away, but it took until 3 p.m. for an additional 100 ballots to be printed and delivered to the site.
Tim Edwards, who lives in Logan Square, said he tried to vote at Goethe Elementary School at 11:30 a.m. and then again around 3 p.m. Both times the polling place, which only has one electric machine, was out of paper ballots. He said he voted at Goethe during the last primary and had no problem.
Jessica Sullivan-Wilson, a volunteer handing out pamphlets outside Goethe for Chicago School Board incumbent Carlos Rivas Jr, said she had been at the polling site since 6 a.m. and said paper ballots ran out twice, once at around 8:15 a.m. and again at 2:30 p.m.
Two electronic voting machines have been delivered to the site, but voting is delayed and volunteers said the site will stay open until everyone votes. Some volunteers are sending people to early voting sites to minimize the line.
Ald. Daniel La Spata (1st) told Block Club he was aware several precincts in his Near Northwest Side ward had run out of paper ballots on Tuesday, including two precincts at Goethe Elementary School running out of those ballots around 9 a.m. — and then running out again this afternoon.
“I’m glad that a lot of election judges are saying that it’s extraordinarily high turnout. That would not explain running out by 9 a.m.,” La Spata said. “The patience that I’ve seen and the professionalism that I’ve seen from election judges is off the chart, but they should have been better resourced for this election. And I’m definitely going to be asking those questions” of the elections board.
Ald. Leni Manaa-Hoppenworth (48th) said she was aware of the ballot situation in her Far North Side ward, and had reached out to the elections board about getting more ballots as well. Her office also brought water bottles and cookies for the neighbors waiting.
Voters in Pilsen also faced over an hour-long wait to cast their votes using the only voting machine at the Manuel Perez Jr. Elementary School Tuesday afternoon. The polling site ran out of paper ballots twice.
Election judge Jesus Fraga said poll workers initially ran out of paper ballots around 10 a.m. and after receiving an additional batch, they ran out again around 3:20 p.m. By then, over 470 people had voted at the site, he said.
After contacting the Board of Elections, Fraga said the site was hoping to get more paper ballots and electronic machines, but he did not know how many.

articles.title_orig: Google Curbs AI in School Accounts After Pushback
articles.title_zh: Google Curbs AI in School Accounts After Pushback
articles.content_orig:
We’re bringing Guided Learning capabilities to Search and Google Classroom, and evolving our approach to school controls.
VP & General Manager, Education
Your browser does not support the audio element.
Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education, is introducing Guided Learning to Google Search and Google Classroom to help students think critically through complex problems. These tools provide step-by-step coaching instead of direct answers to support productive study habits. You can find Guided Learning in Google Classroom today, and we are beginning a pilot program for Search in select U.S. schools later this month.
Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education, explains that we are adding Guided Learning to Google Search and Classroom to help students think through problems instead of just finding quick answers. This tool acts like a personal coach, using questions to guide students through complex topics step by step. We are also giving school administrators full control to decide which AI tools are available to their students, ensuring technology supports classroom learning.
If you’ve ever watched a student use AI tools to help with their schoolwork, you’ve probably wondered: Are they actually learning, or just finding a shortcut? Questions like this are important, and they guide our work when building products for learning.
We believe technology paired with great educators can unlock incredible learning potential, and we’re focused on building technology responsibly to help students thrive. Today, we’re making important updates to our products used in schools, including building Guided Learning capabilities into Google Search and Google Classroom, and evolving our approach to school controls.
We believe AI products should support “productive struggle” — enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up. That’s the philosophy behind Guided Learning. In Gemini, Guided Learning acts as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we’re now bringing Guided Learning to more products.
Google Classroom: Starting today, Guided Learning is globally available in Google Classroom, a central hub where teachers and students organize schoolwork, share assignments and stay connected. When a student starts a Guided Learning activity assigned by their teacher, it acts like a 1-1 study tool, anchored in class material to help them stay on task. It also gives teachers real-time insights to spot where the class might need extra support.
Before launching Guided Learning in Google Classroom, we worked closely with schools and educators to test the feature and integrate their feedback.
We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach. After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.
We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition. Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.
We’ll continue to listen to feedback and evolve our approach as we work in partnership with schools, teachers, pedagogical experts, and parents on helping the next generation learn and thrive.

articles.title_orig: How Wall Street analysts think the midterms could affect the stock market
articles.title_zh: How Wall Street analysts think the midterms could affect the stock market
articles.content_orig:
The midterm elections could reshape Congress as lawmakers grapple with persistent inflation , high energy prices and rising fiscal debt . For investors, by contrast, the political outcome could deliver a boost.
Data from financial firm Edward Jones shows that the S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 1.7% in the month after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970. In the six months following midterm elections, S&P returns averaged 15.5%.
"Volatility around the vote is possible, but markets have historically performed well in the year following midterms as political uncertainty recedes and attention returns to the economic outlook," Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at the global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said in an email on Tuesday as Americans cast their votes.
With congressional control in the balance, Wall Street analysts are also considering the impact divided government could have on stocks if the Democrats win the House, Senate or both chambers. Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to analysts.
"Less change makes a more predictable environment, which allows companies to invest in longer-term projects," Chris Low, chief economist at FHN Financial, a capital markets firm, said in an email Tuesday. "That tends to be good for earnings."
Less stock market volatility doesn't guarantee investors an easy ride, however. Gridlock in Washington, D.C., could also fuel another partisan standoff on the nation's debt, which recently surpassed $40 trillion , or spur the U.S. government to increase its borrowing to fund its priorities, according to economists.
That could unnerve bond investors, who are worried that Washington is on an unsustainable fiscal trajectory, Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, said in a note to investors.
"Prolonged shutdowns and fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher, weighing on equity valuations," he said.
The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, estimates that the U.S. will reach the debt limit again sometime between late winter and midsummer of 2027. At that point, lawmakers will have to decide whether to raise the debt ceiling, temporarily suspend it or risk another government shutdown.
Volatility could also persist if President Trump continues to rely on his executive authority to accomplish his priorities, Yardeni said. In that case, Democrats would have little power to restrain Mr. Trump even if they controlled Congress, he noted.
"Hence, a blue wave could deliver a cold shower for stocks, though we would view a significant selloff as a buying opportunity given the remarkable strength of the economy and corporate earnings," Yardeni said.
A Democratic sweep could have other implications for the economy beyond financial markets. That could include Democrats blocking Trump-appointed regulators, according to Jaret Seiberg, a financial policy analyst and managing director at investment bank TD Cowen.
"They [could] leverage this power to force the President to fill Democratic seats on independent agencies like the FDIC, SEC and CFTC," he said.
A Democratic majority in the Senate would also elevate Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, to head the Senate Banking Committee, giving her more latitude to pass populist legislation, Seiberg added. Warren would replace South Carolina Republican Sen. Tim Scott, who currently chairs the influential panel.
However, lawmakers would still be restricted in what they can do at a federal level, given the president's ability to veto legislation, UBS analysts said in a research note.

articles.title_orig: House Republicans accuse the American Psychological Association of antisemitism, threaten accreditation
articles.title_zh: House Republicans accuse the American Psychological Association of antisemitism, threaten accreditation
articles.content_orig:
An accreditation crisis gives the American Psychological Association a unique opportunity to restore scientific integrity and evidence-based practice over ideology.
Photo: J Studios/DigitalVision via Getty Images
The American Psychological Association, the nation’s largest professional organization for psychologists, could lose its power to accredit educational programs. In late September, a key federal oversight board voted to recommend suspending the APA as a federal accreditor. If the Secretary of Education accepts the recommendation, the APA will lose its status for the first time in the organization’s history.
The vote followed “scathing” third-party comments from practicing psychologists and policy professionals. Critics charged the APA with politicizing its programs, including the embrace of “ critical ” psychotherapies that make dubious assumptions about “gender identity” and label Jews colonial oppressors. The APA’s commitment to social-justice ideology undermines its program quality and nondiscrimination standards , commenters noted , particularly in its failure to address complaints of anti-Semitism.
Finally, a reason to check your email.
Sign up for our free newsletter today.
These issues are just part of a broader pattern of decline. As Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow Colin Wright and Andrew Hartz recently reported , roughly 70 of the 90 panels at a 2026 APA conference had clear ideological agendas, including “loosening/abolishing gender assessment guidelines” for medical transition. The APA also recently elected Candice Hargons—a psychologist who campaigned on a commitment to “dismantle oppressive systems” and dismissed “objectivity” as an enemy of scientific integrity—as its next president.
While the APA’s Commission on Accreditation disagreed with the oversight board’s recommendation, it vowed to address all the issues raised in its hearing and to bring itself into compliance with federal regulations . Taking the Commission at its word, the possible suspension represents a rare opportunity for the APA to reinvigorate its standards and rebuild its organizational culture to promote the interests of psychology trainees and the public they serve—not social-justice ideology.
How can the APA turn its ship around? Some basic reforms include introducing a scientific integrity standard, definitions for what constitutes “unsettled” scientific areas, a revised “non-discrimination” standard, and clearer protocols for navigating program complaints.
First, the APA should recommit itself to open scientific inquiry on controversial issues like gender medicine. That would mean adding “scientific integrity” to its enumerated professional values for accredited programs. Doing so would help ensure that APA-accredited programs create environments where faculty and students can teach and research competing scientific viewpoints in good faith.
Currently, the APA dismisses solid criticism of the weak evidence base for youth gender medicine—which prompted medical practice reversals in countries that had been early adopters—as “ misinformation .” That has to change. Greater tolerance is also needed for research findings that challenge the affirming model of care or the supposed immutability of “gender identity.” Committing the organization to a single approach to treating gender dysphoria renders psychologists ill-equipped to navigate the psychological and developmental nuance required to work with today’s gender-confused youth.
Second, the Commission could introduce benchmarks for what constitutes “contested or unsettled” scientific areas. While the APA requires programs to demonstrate alignment with “the current evidence base” across psychological competencies, its public claims regarding the benefits of youth gender medicine are often based on cherry-picked individual studies that don’t reflect the findings of systematic reviews of evidence that evaluate overall evidence quality. Clear benchmarks would build on the scientific integrity standard by requiring programs to disclose the certainty of the evidence and present credible, competing interpretations where there is disagreement.
The change would benefit the APA by eliminating ambiguity—for example, by defining “unsettled” as open questions about benefits and risks according to the findings of systematic reviews, or when reputable clinical practice guidelines recommend varying approaches to the same issue. Clear benchmarks here would benefit trainees and the Commission, while also protecting the APA reputationally.
A related change would be to make it clear that the organization’s resolutions, testimony, and position statements are not proxies for scientific validity —a use to which they are often put. Nor should deviations from the APA’s conclusions automatically demonstrate an APA program’s noncompliance. The Commission should also consider explicitly distinguishing between advocacy positions and empirical findings through the use of evidence hierarchies .
Psychology students deserve equal treatment and access to APA programs. But the Commission’s “DEI” standards go much further than this guarantee. They would be more effective if presented in the language of a universal, nondiscrimination standard. The APA should not require trainees to agree with their philosophical claims about demographic characteristics like “gender identity.”
Addressing the Commission’s concerns about anti-Semitism poses a different challenge. While APA standards ostensibly already protect Jewish students, explicitly extending these protections to secular Jews is worth considering.
The APA’s anti-Semitism issues, however, are arguably more the result of insufficient enforcement than of inadequate protections. Moreover, the code of federal regulations governing accreditation already requires accreditors to review standards-related complaints—including complaints of anti-Semitism—fairly and promptly.
Clearer timelines for resolving complaints would help, as would establishing formal corrective actions for when programs refuse to investigate credible, standards-related complaints. The Commission could also strengthen existing recordkeeping requirements for how programs assess and resolve such issues, including documenting any corrective measures taken.
If the Commission on Accreditation is serious about the government’s concerns, these recommendations are low-hanging fruit. These revised standards are already consistent with the values and spirit of existing accreditation standards and would buttress them in ways that are aligned with the Commission’s quality standards and emphasis on education that serves the interests of patients and future psychologists.
In an era defined by public distrust in institutions, the APA has a rare opportunity to stand up for scientific integrity, evidence-based practice, and equal access. For the sake of patients and trainees, let’s hope that it seizes it.
Joseph Figliolia is a policy analyst at Manhattan Institute.

articles.title_zh: Two helicopters collide near Mount Everest during rescue flight, killing one, injuring others
articles.content_orig:
Video captures the moment two helicopters collide while trying to land at Pheriche Helipad in Nepal and the aftermath of the deadly accident.
Two helicopters collided while attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp in Nepal.
The accident happened at about 8:12 a.m. Tuesday in the Pheriche area of Solukhumbu District, according to a translated press release from the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN). The helicopters were identified as an Air Dynasty aircraft and a Fishtail Air aircraft, the aviation authority said.
Two foreign tourists were aboard the Fishtail Air helicopter. One of them, 47-year-old Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu of Chennai, India, died in the accident, according to CAAN.
DEADLY HELICOPTER CRASH KILLS 2 PILOTS BATTLING RAGING WILDFIRE IN YOSEMITE
The other tourist, New Zealand national Shailesh Kisan Patel, was injured, along with at least one pilot involved in the collision, the authority said.
Those injured in the collision were admitted to a hospital in Kathmandu for further treatment, according to the aviation authority.
The two helicopters pictured above collided while attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp in Nepal. (Reuters)
CAAN has opened an investigation into the accident and will determine whether corrective action is needed based on its findings.
Fishtail Air said its helicopter crashed during landing while transporting passengers rescued from the Everest region , Reuters reported.

The Air Dynasty helicopter was carrying only cargo, an official with the company told Reuters.
Helicopters are a key form of transportation around Everest, where there are no roads. They are used to evacuate trekkers and guides suffering from illness or exhaustion amid the region's cold temperatures and high altitude, according to The Associated Press (AP).
The two helicopters shown above collided with each other while attempting to land near Mount Everest base camp in Nepal. (Viral Press)
Pheriche, where the accident occurred, sits about 13,780 feet above sea level and is located below Everest base camp, the AP reported.
The collision also came after heavy snow had covered trekking routes in the region.
Conditions improved Sunday, allowing thousands of trekkers to begin moving through the area again, according to the outlet.

Nepal has faced other major travel and safety challenges in recent months.
In September, about 70 Americans remained unaccounted for following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, while 18 Americans had been confirmed safe, Fox News Digital previously reported.
A damaged helicopter sits after two helicopters collided as they prepared to land in Nepal's Mount Everest region on Nov. 3, 2026. (Reuters)
The flooding was triggered by an Aug. 26 glacier collapse and caused widespread destruction, including flash floods and landslides. Rescue crews were searching areas, including hydropower project tunnels, where workers were believed to be trapped.

U.S. officials warned Americans at the time not to travel to the disaster zone because of the continued threat of additional flash floods and landslides.
At least 1,399 people across Nepal and China's Tibet region died in the disaster, with more than 5,400 others still missing at the time of the report.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft improves Windows 11 performance on 8 GB PCs as RAM prices keep climbing
articles.title_zh: Microsoft improves Windows 11 performance on 8 GB PCs as RAM prices keep climbing
articles.content_orig:
We've got a hunch the memory crunch is taking a bite out of Windows revenue
With RAM getting more expensive, Microsoft is putting more effort into making Windows 11 run better on systems with just 8 GB of memory.
Microsoft said on Tuesday that it was "raising the bar for 8 GB Windows 11 PCs," following a renewed focus on memory optimization earlier this year . The changes come as Redmond continues pushing more expensive Copilot+ PCs, which require at least 16 GB of RAM, amid a memory crunch fueled by AI infrastructure demand.
Now, Microsoft says a low-end machine with its 8 GB of precious RAM will be up to 20 percent more responsive and 40 percent faster at multitasking thanks to improvements made in memory management.
The tweaks are relatively simple, as Microsoft explained, and seem more about adjusting back to the reality that its flagship operating system needs to function on the hardware people can actually afford to purchase if and when they’re forced to upgrade.
Windows 11 will now keep up to 2 GB more active data in memory before shunting it to slower storage, as one example. In another instance, Windows will connect directly to Edge when the browser is already running in the background, allowing it to launch up to 33 percent faster, according to Microsoft. Microsoft apps are also being made more efficient, with Teams able to enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which Microsoft said will make it launch "up to 20 percent faster."
Memory efficiency is also being improved by tweaking things like Widgets, which will only load when used instead of always being on, and decreasing the time when Edge tabs go to sleep from two hours to 15 minutes by default. Microsoft said it’s enabling third-party apps to make use of those tweaks, too.
Microsoft also included benchmark data in the blog post from a recent bit of research it commissioned. The benchmark report compares a range of 2026 Windows machines with models from 2021, finding that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8 GB of RAM performed about as well as a 2021 Dell XPS 13 with 16 GB across selected workloads.
What that means, says Microsoft, is that “the complete PC, not memory capacity alone, shapes the experience.”
In other words, please buy some new Windows hardware, even if it’s expensive - we’re begging you. Software optimization can only do so much.
“For many people, 8 GB is a great fit for the things they do every day,” Microsoft EVP of Windows and devices Pavan Davuluri wrote in the blog post. “Demanding workloads, such as 3D modeling, advanced video editing, or large-scale data processing benefit from 16 GB of memory or more.”
It’s no surprise Microsoft is improving the performance of lower end systems at the same time it’s subtly asking users to buy newer kit, even if it’s just an 8 GB machine - Microsoft may have done well in the past two quarters, but it’s no thanks to Windows devices.
Microsoft’s Q4 2026 earnings in late July saw the company rake in cash more broadly, while simultaneously reporting a 7 percent decrease in Windows OEM and devices revenue.
Likewise, in its fiscal Q1 2027 results, reported just last week, Microsoft again brought home a mountain of net income, with adjusted earnings reaching $36.4 billion, up 18 percent from the same period last year. Windows OEM and devices revenue, however, was down a whopping 22 percent . It’s hard to think of a reason beyond the fact that hardware prices have shot up with more force than a SpaceX rocket - memory prices are likely to actually make it to Mars, unlike Starship - leaving both consumers and enterprises to stretch those upgrade cycles.
If you need to get the most out of that 8 GB Windows 11 PC, you’ll find the latest improvements in 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later. Microsoft is also encouraging users to keep its branded apps up to date, as “some improvements arrive through app updates or through Microsoft Store.”  ®

articles.content_orig:

Nov 3 (Reuters) - The Nasdaq ended higher on Tuesday as AI heavyweights rebounded ahead of US midterm election results, while Apple fell after the iPhone maker joined the list of Big Tech companies whose quarterly results failed ‌to impress investors.
Apple dropped 1.9% after it warned that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring its ‌holiday-quarter gross margin.
Memory-chip maker Micron Technology gained 2.6%, while Nvidia rose 2.3% after falling in the last four sessions.
The broader Philadelphia chips index jumped, while AMD rose ahead of ​its quarterly report due after the bell.
Microsoft and Amazon each moved more than 2% higher.
"This is a rotation from safe tech, like Apple, into riskier tech, like chipmakers," said Jay Hatfield, chief executive officer at Infrastructure Capital Management. "It's clear dip-buying in a higher-risk, Nasdaq-driven market."
The Nasdaq 100 on Monday ended more than 10% below its October 6 record-high close, confirming that the tech-heavy index has entered a correction as investors worry that massive investments ‌in AI infrastructure are outpacing near-term cash generation.
Shares ⁠of Amazon and Alphabet fell sharply last week after their quarterly results deepened investors' concerns about the cost of heavy AI spending.
The S&P 500 is down about 3% from its record-high close on October 6, and it ⁠remains up over 10% in 2026.
Oil prices eased as investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries about additional supply disruptions from recent attacks in both conflicts. Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official ​told ​Reuters.
The S&P 500 climbed 0.36% to end the session at 7,568.92 points.
The Nasdaq ​gained 0.83% to 25,372.01 points, while the Dow Jones ‌Industrial Average declined 0.38% to 51,787.04 points.
Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by consumer staples, down 1.76%, followed by a 1.75% loss in materials.

American voters will deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump's second term in Tuesday's midterm elections, with polls and nonpartisan analysts favoring Democrats to wrest the House from Republicans, while control of the Senate ‌remains uncertain.

articles.title_zh: Google Messages redesigning pinned chats and moving search
articles.content_orig:
In addition to the new app icon , Google Messages is testing a redesign of pinned chats and search on the homepage.
Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.
This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s currently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.
You’ll see large contact photos appear above all chats, which pushes the list of other conversations down the page. Like iMessage on iOS, this layout has the downside of not showing any history or last sent information.
Meanwhile, Google is testing another change where search becomes a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside new chat. When you’re scrolling down the page, you’ll see “Search” in a pill-shaped button, with the other button minimized.
Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive.
This is a nice change for one-handed usage. It’s unclear if Google is removing the Gemini FAB with this update.
These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to testers.
