articles.title_zh: Hiding inside Palantir’s skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
The data analysis company Palantir delivered such a huge third-quarter earnings report on Monday that its press release even bragged that the numbers were “crushing consensus expectations.”
Yet retail investors were lukewarm on the company on Tuesday, with the stock trading slightly down. That’s because Palantir’s enterprise sales, its big growth area, showed signs of slowing.
First, the good news for the company’s investors. Revenue grew 96% from a year earlier, and 20% from the previous quarter, to $2.31 billion, beating analysts’ expectations of $2.18 billion. It was the first time Palantir has topped $2 billion in a quarter. Palantir also reported adjusted earnings per share (profit per share, excluding certain one-time items) of 44 cents, compared with analysts’ expectations of 41 cents. The company even raised its revenue guidance, or forecast, for the full year. Normally, that alone would send a stock soaring.
The clincher was that Palantir’s U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time ever. The company reported $984 million in commercial contracts (up 148% from the year-ago quarter), versus $953 million in U.S. government revenue.
The reason for all this love from enterprises? They are signing up for the company’s AI software that can run frontier models and custom-train open-weight models securely, without sharing any of their data and business processes with outside AI labs. Plus, Palantir has long offered what is today known as “forward-deployed” software engineering, in which its own engineers work directly with customers to customize the software.
However, Palantir also revealed a less-than-rosy signal: Even as enterprises are moving faster than ever, they are often signing short-term trials.
“What Ryan and I are seeing on the front line and commercial is this much quicker interaction, much quicker to deployment, shorter duration of the contract but then an ability to expand that contract dramatically,” CEO Alex Karp (pictured above) told Wall Street analysts on the quarterly earnings call.
Palantir is experiencing one of the unique phenomena of AI in the enterprise right now. Corporations are willing to quickly try AI software, skipping the usual bureaucracy, but they are also more willing to cancel contracts.
Karp used one off-color metaphor after another to describe how unconcerned he was about holding onto his enterprise business.
“We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team, kind of thing,” he said, describing the influx of prospective corporate customers flowing in. “Conversely, you know, once you go Palantir, you don’t go back, and that’s just how it is, and you see it in our numbers.”
The numbers don’t yet confirm Palantir’s long-term success. While the company closed a hefty $1.46 billion of total contract value from U.S. enterprises in the quarter, that’s actually a decline from the record $2.13 billion in the previous quarter. That suggests slowing sales, at least in the most recent quarter.
The next earnings will show whether Palantir has solidified its role as a rising U.S. enterprise AI provider. Historically, many enterprises sign their biggest tech purchases in the final quarter of the year. Karp and his team certainly sound confident. They increased guidance for U.S. commercial revenue to be “in excess of $3.559 billion, representing a growth rate of at least 143%.”

articles.title_orig: Spanish transport minister resigns after two deadly train crashes in one year
articles.title_zh: Spanish transport minister resigns after two deadly train crashes in one year
articles.content_orig:
Spain’s Minister of Transport Óscar Puente announced his resignation after two deadly train crashes occurred in a single year, including one last week that killed 69 people and injured more than 200.
“I made the decision about my future in the first few minutes after the tragedy,” Puente told lawmakers in Madrid. “A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this severity in less than a year, however different they may be and regardless of whether or not they bear direct responsibility for them.”
Puente resigned six days after one train plowed into another after what authorities say was a combination of human and computer errors along a high speed railway line connecting Madrid and Andalusia. One train, operated by Spain’s national rail service, crashed into a stationary train at high speed during a safety system failure that had halted all rail traffic along the line.
“There was a red signal prohibiting movement, yet the train was authorized to proceed,” Puente said last week. “It is a decision made under inexplicable circumstances.”
Last week’s crash was preceded by another serious rail accident in January, where two high-speed trains collided head-on in the town of Adamuz, killing at least 41 people. At the time, it was the deadliest crash Spain had seen in more than a decade.
Numerous politicians and Spain’s transport workers’ union had called on Puente to resign in the aftermath of last week’s collision. The night of the crash, police scuffled with a hundreds of protesters outside the transport ministry headquarters, some of whom carried placards demanding that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez resign.
Puente’s announcement arrives just three weeks before the country’s general elections, in which the minister said he would not be standing as a candidate. Sánchez called those elections early in the wake of several corruption scandals, a controversy over housing affordability and numerous setbacks for his socialist PSOE party in municipal elections.
Sánchez praised Puente in a statement on social media, saying that the former transport minister stepped aside “out of respect for the victims and the progressive project.”
“Politicians like him dignify our country and show us that not all of us are the same,” Sánchez wrote. “While some only give lessons, others give everything.”

articles.title_orig: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
articles.title_zh: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
articles.content_orig:
King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.
There have been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also at the summit, has said that he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations.
While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.
He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.
"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."
He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."
King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.
"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."
The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.
The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Speaking on Tuesday, Burnham said his government was bringing a new approach, aiming to "revitalise the Commonwealth", despite turning down demands for reparations.
"I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," he said.
"But it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they've got, green finance.
"That's what we've done under all governments and in my view we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth."
The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

articles.title_orig: JetBlue raises bag fees for third time in a year as fuel costs bite
articles.title_zh: JetBlue raises bag fees for third time in a year as fuel costs bite
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to the era of the $70 bag fee.
JetBlue Airways has raised the price of checking a bag for many customers for the third time in less than a year as high fuel costs continue to eat into the industry's profits.
Checking a first bag for travelers booked in economy will now be $50, up from $45, if purchased more than 24 hours before departure during a nonpeak travel period. If it's paid within 24 hours of departure, the fee will be $60. During a peak period, such as during the holidays or the summer, it will be $55 if purchased more than 24 hours before departure, up from $49, and $70 for within 24 hours of departure.
There are exceptions to the checked bag fees, such as for customers who hold a co-branded JetBlue credit card or who hold elite frequent flyer status.
"We're adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in a statement. "This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
The price of jet fuel, airlines' biggest cost after labor, has roughly doubled this year since the start of the Iran war in February, costing airlines billions and driving up the price of tickets. Jet fuel was going for $4.44 a gallon on Tuesday for the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Other airlines often follow when one carrier raises fees. Major U.S. airlines did so earlier this year after JetBlue raised its bag fees.
The changes were reported earlier by the Thrifty Traveler blog .

articles.title_orig: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue
articles.title_zh: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue
articles.content_orig:
CrowdStrike is betting that it has a solution to rogue artificial intelligence .
The cybersecurity vendor on Tuesday launched an AI kill switch designed to let security teams stop internal AI agents that go rogue, block them from relaunching and cut off their enterprise network access. The tool is built into CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian platform, launched in September to secure AI agents. CrowdStrike also announced an integration with Anthropic's Claude Cowork .
"Having the ability to control and turn off, and make a decision and decide, I think that's really important for this next chapter of AI adoption," Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard told CNBC.
A string of recent high-profile cyber incidents has added urgency to calls for some kind of emergency shutdown mechanism.
The Hugging Face breach orchestrated by rogue OpenAI agents in July was particularly alarming for businesses. Last week, Binance disclosed the largest crypto cyberattack on record and hackers have recently targeted hundreds of refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in France.
Over the summer, U.S. representatives introduced bipartisan legislation that would require AI companies to build shutdown capabilities into their models.
Critics argue, however, that an emergency stop button is far too complicated to implement across multiple systems, data centers and complex AI models.
Bernard said the kill switch operates like a circuit breaker in systems where customers use its Falcon platform. The process can detect internal agent activity but requires a human to decide to cut the agent off and reinstate access.
"If you kill a process at the root, and we have that level of access at the root … it's very binary," Bernard said. "You either kill the AI and the agent, or you don't, and then you report on that."
The kill switch doesn't delete the agent's code but uses connected AI gateways to cut off access to the AI models that influence decisions, CrowdStrike said.
In the age of AI, businesses are moving quickly to adopt autonomous tools, often without the necessary safeguards and protections.
CrowdStrike believes its new tool will let companies stop AI agent 'misbehavior in its tracks, while leaving room for innovation.
The company also announced plans to acquire AI observability startup Fiddler AI and AI security testing firm Dreadnode .
CrowdStrike and its rivals are rapidly scooping up cybersecurity startups to keep up with increasing security demands. The need for AI security tools has also powered a broader wave of cybersecurity deal-making .

articles.title_orig: JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!
articles.title_zh: JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!
articles.content_orig:
For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees , and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…
Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees . JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.
Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.
As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.
It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.
When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.
The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.
JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027 , though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:
JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.
When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

articles.title_orig: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
articles.title_zh: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
articles.content_orig:
Binance released on Tuesday a detailed investigation into the $6 billion hack of its cryptocurrency platform, showing how attackers used fake job interviews and malicious code to steal the funds.
The crypto exchange said it had replenished 98 percent of the affected assets by drawing on its own funds, with the remaining amount involving little-traded currencies that are harder to acquire.
The attack, carried out over about four hours on October 29, was attributed by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to North Korea-affiliated hackers.
Pyongyang has denied the allegations, with the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un calling the claim "absurd rhetoric."
Around $2.85 billion of the stolen $6.34 billion has been frozen, Binance said, meaning that the attackers could not use it or convert it to another currency.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply.
According to Binance, attackers took their first steps towards the breach as early as June.
First, they targeted a platform engineer by getting them to download a virus-laden version of the widely-known programming software Homebrew.
Binance's cybersecurity teams identified the malware and removed it, but the hackers had already had time to harvest information about the engineer and his colleagues.
In September, the attackers approached another Binance engineer through a legitimate job-search platform, offering him an interview for a position in a fictitious company.
After building trust with the subject through the sharing of social media photos and videos, they asked the engineer to download a test exercise as part of the interview process.
The exercise contained malware that deployed "sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques," Binance said, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version.
That malware was critical to the success of the attack, as it allowed the hackers to establish a connection with Binance's internal systems.
On October 20, the attackers used the access they had gained and an internal AI tool to gain control over software used by two other engineers.
Nine days later, they triggered malicious code that initiated the attack.

articles.title_orig: China seeks APEC solutions to world development ahead of leaders’ summit
articles.title_zh: China seeks APEC solutions to world development ahead of leaders’ summit
articles.content_orig:
China on Tuesday urged Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) members to continue contributing practical and effective "Asia-Pacific solutions" to the region's and the world's development, according to media reports.
Top diplomat Wang Yi highlighted the importance of the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting later this month in an address to the 37th Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Ministerial Meeting via video conference, state-run Xinhua News reported.
Wang, who co-chaired the meeting with Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, said Beijing is willing to work with "all parties" to do a "good job" in the final stage of the 2026 APEC "China Year" and contribute to the fruitful results at the leaders' meeting.
He said the leaders' meeting is an "important one" concerning the future development of the Asia-Pacific region.
The commerce minister urged all APEC parties to uphold free trade and innovation-driven development, foster a vibrant engine for growth, advance discussions and policy coordination on digital and intelligent economic and trade rules, and build a fair and equitable international economic and trade order.
China will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in south China in November. It will mark the country's third time hosting the event, following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.
The theme of the summit is "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together.” China has identified openness, innovation and cooperation as the three priority areas for this year's APEC cooperation.

articles.title_orig: What the midterm elections could mean for markets, debt
articles.title_zh: What the midterm elections could mean for markets, debt
articles.content_orig:
‘Varney & Co.’ host Stuart Varney examines a potential socialist surge, Republican upsets in red states and what an election shakeup could mean for Congress and Wall Street.
Voters across America are casting their ballots in the midterm elections on Tuesday, which will determine control of Congress and could add to investors' concerns about oversight of the artificial intelligence (AI) sector and how the debt ceiling will be addressed next year.
Since President Donald Trump's second term began in 2025 with Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress, the S&P 500 has gained about 27% in part due to a massive influx of spending on AI and strong earnings growth.
Treasury yields are also significantly higher in part because of geopolitical risks that emerged with the outbreak of the Iran war in late February, which caused a surge in energy prices. U.S. budget deficits have continued to widen to about $2 trillion, adding more upward pressure to yields as debt issuance mounts.
Investors are weighing how the results of the election will affect the outlook for financial markets depending on whether Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress.
AFFORDABILITY TAKES CENTER STAGE AS AMERICANS CAST THEIR BALLOTS IN HIGH-STAKES MIDTERMS
The midterm elections will determine control of Congress for the next two years, carrying implications for the nation's finances and markets. (J. David Ake/Getty Images)
Since 1930, there have been eight midterm cycles when the president's party lost control of the House, and the S&P 500 rose for the remainder of the year five times, Ned Davis Research said. It posted a median gain of 1.4% from Election Day through year-end, slightly less than the 1.9% posted across all post-Election Day midterm years.
In a scenario in which Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress , investors expect tougher oversight of AI which could weigh on markets that have been pushed higher by the emerging tech.
Democratic majorities would have the ability to investigate corporate America while attempting to slow deregulation , which could increase market volatility.
DSA PLATFORM COULD COST UP TO $212T OVER A DECADE, ANALYSIS FINDS
Markets have generally fared well under divided government. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
If Democrats win the House but Republicans hold their majority in the Senate, implications for the U.S. fiscal situation could be mixed.
Bipartisan compromises would be required over issues like funding the government to avoid shutdowns and raising the debt ceiling , which could create the potential for brinkmanship.
In a scenario where Republicans retain their majorities in the House and Senate, the GOP could pursue further tax reforms or boost defense spending.
FEDERAL BUDGET DEFICIT HITS $2T AS NATIONAL DEBT COSTS SURGE
The results of the midterms will impact negotiations between Congress and the Trump administration depending on who controls the House and Senate. (Grant Baldwin/AFP via Getty Images)
Ned Davis chief U.S. strategist Ed Clissold said that a House takeover by Democrats could modestly temper the U.S. equity market's year-end rally, but in general it hasn't prevented stocks from advancing.
"Conventional wisdom is that gridlock is good (for stocks)," said Clissold, adding that stocks have performed better under Democratic presidents than Republicans.
Diego Barnuevo, market analyst at Ebury, said that a Democratic-held Congress' negotiations with the White House would likely be limited to the budget and debt ceiling, and that a "Democratic sweep would be neutral to mildly positive for the fiscal outlook."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A Republican sweep could ease concerns over investigations into AI companies that carry the potential to rattle markets.
"If Republicans maintain control of Congress, that would likely provide the most supportive incremental federal policy backdrop for the AI/infrastructure buildout through policy continuity, potential fiscal expansion, deregulation and faster federal permitting," JPMorgan strategists said in a note.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI
articles.title_zh: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI
articles.content_orig:
Google announced Tuesday morning that it would switch off AI products by default for students in schools that use the technology giant’s education software. But those schools that forgo its AI services would also be cut off from Google Search.
The move comes after mounting criticism from advocacy groups and senators about the spread of Google’s AI services available in classrooms. Until Tuesday, its AI products — branded under the Gemini moniker — were automatically activated for schools using Google Classroom.
Google said Tuesday’s move would also cut off students’ access to Google Search if schools do not enable Gemini, given AI’s growing integration into the company’s search products.
Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post announcing the change that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search “will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Phillips wrote.
Some education and technology advocates immediately slammed the decision, painting the move as a punishment for schools that don’t use Google’s AI. “It is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of our children,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, a national educators union.
“Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether,” she told NBC News in written comments.
Josh Golin, executive director of advocacy group Fairplay, said in a statement that Google is attempting “to strong-arm schools into using its AI products.”
“Schools should use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click,” Golin said.
In a statement posted to social media after this article was published, Google said the announcements “give schools more choice, not less,” and that schools can turn on Google Search individually without enabling Gemini products. But Search will still have AI features built into it, which the company said have been updated “to make it better for learning. Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.”
Earlier this year, Google turned on Gemini in its Classroom app, allowing children — regardless of age — to access AI products unless districts disabled it .
Parent advocacy groups and experts on the use of technology in schools denounced Google for providing AI products to children — raising concern that students would outsource their work to AI systems on school devices — and lobbied school districts to disable Gemini products. In an open letter in early October, 13 leading parent advocacy organizations — including the Digital Childhood Institute and Schools Beyond Screens — called on school districts to turn off access to Gemini and YouTube, which is also owned by Google .
Google has established a dominant role in education technology over the past 15 years. The vast majority of Chromebook laptops are purchased by school districts to provide to students. Nearly two-thirds of assignments use a Google product, according to a 2023 report by the firm Schoolytics. This year, the company began offering multiday AI trainings for educators, featuring sessions that focused on how they could mitigate pushback by teachers who don’t want to use AI.
Research on AI in educational settings has not established a long-term benefit for students. There are no high-quality causal studies into student use of AI, according to the SCALE Initiative at the Stanford Graduate School of Education . Researchers have also warned that many of the studies conducted so far on AI in education didn’t measure whether it boosted learning and often did not test whether AI-assisted learning was superior to other teaching methods.
In Tuesday’s blog post , Google said that for schools that enable the company’s AI products, they will now detect when a student is trying to use them just to get an answer on an assignment. A redesigned version of Google Search will instead walk students through the topic or problem and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer, the company said.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.
Tyler Kingkade is a national reporter for NBC News, based in Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
articles.title_zh: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
articles.content_orig:
The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.
“Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere,” the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that “Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission,” while “publishers have received nothing.”
The lawsuit said, “AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index,” and use content from the Brave index “to train their own AI models” and “to respond to specific user queries.” The NYT lawsuit points to Brave’s website , which says the Brave Search API is “used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com.”
The lawsuit accused Brave of all the major types of copyright infringement: direct infringement, contributory infringement, and vicarious infringement. The lawsuit claims Brave infringes copyrights directly by scraping articles for its search index, for its “Ask Brave” AI search feature, and for the Brave API that “serves as an illicit source of unlicensed copyrighted material, including Times journalism, to other AI companies.”
The NYT accused Brave of being “a contributory and vicarious infringer when it deliberately induces, facilitates, controls, and profits from its users’ and GenAI customers’ copying of the copyrighted content.” Finally, the lawsuit said Brave violated the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) by circumventing technological measures the NYT and other content owners use to restrict access to their articles.
“The Brave Browser includes a default setting that, when activated, causes the browser to go behind website paywalls and provide the paywalled content to the user,” the lawsuit said. The browser “blocks advertising that would otherwise appear on The Times’s website, and instead shows its own ads, offering its users a cut of the revenue even as it deprives The Times of digital advertising revenue that helps it fund the expensive effort of producing journalism,” the lawsuit said.
When testing the Brave browser for Mac today, we found that the optional “paywall blocker” feature made it possible to read a paywalled New York Times article. The feature was enabled in the default settings and can be turned off.
The NYT asked for a permanent injunction to stop Brave from continuing the allegedly illegal conduct. The lawsuit seeks statutory damages, actual damages, restitution of profits derived from alleged copyright infringement, and “restitution and disgorgement of all revenue and profits Brave obtained through its ad-substitution scheme.”
A similar lawsuit was filed against Brave in the same court yesterday by the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel companies. We contacted Brave and will update this article if it provides a response.
Perplexity, which is not a defendant in the Brave lawsuit but is facing a different lawsuit filed by the NYT, accused the news organization of “disinformation” in a statement provided to Ars and other news outlets. Perplexity’s statement did not identify any specific inaccuracies in the lawsuit against Brave.
“The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.),” Perplexity’s statement said.
The NYT sued Perplexity in December 2025, alleging that its AI tool gives users “outputs that are identical or substantially similar to” NYT articles, including “verbatim or near-verbatim reproductions, summaries, or abridgements of the original content.” Perplexity’s response to that lawsuit said its answer engine only fetches content from copyrighted articles in reply to user queries. Perplexity argued that “developing an AI tool that can allegedly automatically fetch and provide specific content in response to user requests based on its pre-configuration and access to materials available on the Internet” is not “volitional conduct.”
The NYT also sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023 in a lawsuit alleging that OpenAI trains its AI with stolen news content. The lawsuit is heading toward a trial , with OpenAI arguing that its use of news articles is fair use under copyright law.

articles.title_orig: China’s HQ-9B air defense system destroys maneuvering missile in tests
articles.title_zh: China’s HQ-9B air defense system destroys maneuvering missile in tests
articles.content_orig:
Authorities in Beijing announced that the PLA Air Force utilized the HQ-9B surface-to-air missile platform to successfully neutralize targets during a training drill. These objectives consisted of missiles capable of rapid movement and complex maneuvering.
The evaluations of the HQ-9B, a modern addition to the Chinese military inventory, required the interception of two distinct missile varieties. One specific target executed an abrupt mid-air pivot before plummeting toward the earth at extreme velocity.
According to the state media outlet China Central Television (CCTV), the Central Theater Command's Shenwei Missile Battalion within the PLA Air Force carried out the maneuvers.
Personnel from the Shenwei Missile Battalion were not briefed on the specific nature of the incoming threats; they were informed only that the mission involved engaging agile, high-velocity projectiles.
A battalion participant noted that the crew was afforded a mere two-second window to react. In this brief interval, they were required to identify the mysterious object and determine if a launch was necessary.
Military specialist Song Zhongping remarked, in a report by the Global Times , that despite precise radar monitoring, a defense system must possess the capacity for mid-flight trajectory adjustments to successfully follow a target exhibiting erratic flight patterns.
For guidance and tracking during an engagement, the HQ-9B utilizes an active radar homing (ARH) mechanism paired with an inertial navigation system (INS). Beyond its sophisticated steering and engine technologies, the HQ-9B is capable of striking targets that follow non-linear flight paths. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of a missile intercept is contingent upon multiple variables, such as communication reliability, target velocity, reaction speed, and radar precision.
The drill also showcased the PLA's ability to fuse different missile, command, and radar elements into a cohesive air defense web. Expert Song Zhongping clarified that China has established a unified data-sharing architecture for its diverse air defense branches to distribute intelligence on approaching hazards and synchronize their actions. Threats are distributed among various units depending on their proximity and combat readiness.
Hu Yang, another member of the battalion, mentioned that just two minutes elapse between the reception of a high-level warning and the actual interception. While the drill proves the HQ-9B can hit maneuvering missiles, its capacity to stop hypersonic cruise missiles or glide vehicles requires separate validation through authentic combat simulations.
Although the HQ-9B might intercept a target approaching directly, engaging hypersonic cruise missiles or glide vehicles presents an extreme challenge for any surface-to-air hardware. Testing the HQ-9B against maneuvering aerial targets does not verify its effectiveness against operational hypersonic technology. Assessing the system's utility against such weaponry would require distinct trials in practical operational settings.
Earlier, during September 2025, China exhibited numerous air defense assets . Featured hardware included the HQ-29, HQ-19, HQ-9C, and HQ-9B. These platforms represent China's expanding proficiency in defending against diverse missile types and fixed-wing aircraft.
The latest HQ-9B drills highlight the ongoing technical advancement of China's armed forces. Still, the ability of the system to negate sophisticated missile hazards remains unproven until subjected to independent testing in lifelike combat scenarios.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Claims of Iranian Chemical Weapons Divide U.S. Officials
articles.title_zh: Israeli Claims of Iranian Chemical Weapons Divide U.S. Officials
articles.content_orig:
Israel has provided the United States with intelligence indicating that Iran is considering using chemical weapons against its adversaries, but officials in Washington are divided over the information's credibility and significance, The New York Times reported on Tuesday, citing American and regional officials.
Some senior US officials received the intelligence with concern, while others expressed deep skepticism, viewing it as part of a pressure campaign by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government aimed at convincing the Trump administration to resume large-scale fighting against Iran .
According to the report, during discussions with US intelligence agencies and other officials over the past two weeks, senior Israeli officials presented the chemical weapons threat as more urgent than Iran's ambitions to develop nuclear weapons.
Israeli intelligence officials told their American counterparts that they believe Iran is rapidly advancing technology that would allow it to mount chemical weapons on missiles or smuggle them into Israel or another country to carry out an attack.
Other senior American officials believe the threat should be taken seriously, particularly in light of a series of recent warnings about Iranian preparations to attack US interests.
According to the newspaper, there is little disagreement within the American intelligence community that Iran is developing chemical weapons. The central dispute concerns whether Iranian leaders would actually use them, particularly if Iran is not attacked again.
Israel also shared some of the intelligence with officials in Gulf states. Several questioned whether Iran was developing plans to use chemical weapons and believe Israel is attempting to push the United States and its partners toward a more intensive phase of the war.
A regional official told the newspaper that Israel had presented Gulf countries with assessments suggesting Iran was working to make its chemical weapons operational, but had not shared supporting evidence.
According to the official, Gulf governments regarded the claims as lacking seriousness.
For some American officials, the warnings have revived memories of the faulty intelligence surrounding Iraq's weapons of mass destruction in 2002.
At the time, US intelligence agencies presented the White House with a firm assessment that Iraq possessed such weapons, although the country had largely abandoned or suspended its nuclear, chemical and biological weapons programs.
Even among those briefed on the new intelligence, assessments differ regarding how quickly and effectively Iran could deploy chemical weapons.
According to experts and American officials who spoke with the newspaper, mounting a chemical weapon on a ballistic missile is not particularly difficult, but ensuring the effective dispersal of the chemical agent is more complicated.
Smuggling a bomb across a border also presents difficulties. Another possibility mentioned was the use of a drone.
Despite the Israeli warnings, the newspaper reported that preparations for responding to chemical weapons attacks are not a central component of the Home Front Command exercises taking place across Israel this week.
Two Home Front Command officials said there had also been no widespread reminders distributed to officers or the public regarding protective instructions against such a threat.
The IDF declined to comment.
The intelligence was shared as the United States and Iran explore the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough while simultaneously preparing for a resumption of hostilities.
According to senior American officials, US Central Command (CENTCOM) has a plan for an attack on Iran that could be carried out as early as Wednesday, November 4, one day after the US midterm elections.
The report stated that three American aircraft carriers are currently in the region, while the preferred operational window for an attack is expected to be brief.
One of the aircraft carriers will need to return to its home port after the beginning of November, and particularly dark nights are expected in the coming days, providing favorable conditions for military operations.
However, President Donald Trump has not yet approved a large-scale attack, and diplomatic contacts between Washington and Tehran are continuing.
In recent weeks, the United States has concentrated warships, fighter jets and bombers in the region in preparation for a possible relatively short military campaign involving intensive strikes.
At the same time, diplomats are attempting to formulate an agreement that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, address Iran's nuclear program and postpone further military action.
According to the report, the military buildup could also serve as leverage to support the diplomatic effort.
Meanwhile, US intelligence agencies assess that the threat to Americans in the Middle East and several other countries is at its highest level since the war began in February.
Intelligence collection was intensified after an Iranian plot to attack a base in Britain used by American fighter jets was uncovered.
On October 23, a warning memorandum regarding potential Iranian attacks was sent to senior administration officials. Diplomats and other personnel were subsequently placed on heightened alert.
The newspaper also linked Netanyahu's efforts to his political situation following the Israeli elections, in which he failed to secure a clear path toward forming a government.
Several commentators who spoke with the newspaper suggested that Netanyahu might attempt to use a national security emergency to pressure opposition leaders into joining a coalition under his leadership.
American allegations regarding an Iranian chemical weapons program date back decades.
In 2003, Iran acknowledged that it had developed chemical capabilities during the Iran-Iraq War but claimed that it subsequently dismantled them.
Tehran denies possessing chemical weapons and has previously described such accusations as psychological warfare conducted by Israel and Netanyahu .
Dana Stroul, a former senior Pentagon official responsible for Middle East policy during the Biden administration, said it has been known for more than two decades that Iran has been stockpiling components for chemical weapons, but has never used them.
However, she warned that Tehran could feel "existential pressure" and potentially cross the threshold into directly using such weapons offensively.
A spokesperson for Netanyahu's office told the NYT : "Israel closely monitors every threat posed by the Iranian terrorist regime and is prepared to confront it."
The White House did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment, but an American official said Trump would defend the United States and its allies against any potential threat.

articles.title_orig: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.title_zh: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.content_orig:
More than 50 people are feared to be trapped under the rubble
Russian strikes on Ukraine â including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital â have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours.
At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.
He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".
Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.
The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.
Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.
Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof  collapsed, trapping many underneath.
"The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen.
However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.
The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment.
According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital.
But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law" , external .
Dozens of terminally ill patients had to evacuate their hospice after it was hit
Further north, in Dnipro, nearly 50 terminally ill patients were being transferred to other facilities after their hospice was destroyed by a Russian missile on Monday night. The oldest of the patients was 90 years old.
Mayor Boris Filatov posted photos on Telegram showing elderly people lying in their beds in a hospice room with blown-out windows and rubble and broken glass strewn on the floors.
Last month, the UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine were at a 'record level'
"I realise that I am violating ethics," wrote Filatov. "I want as many people as possible to see these photos. Especially politicians and diplomats. Especially abroad.
"These are elderly, terminally ill people. This is a Russian missile."
Elsewhere in Dnipro, a separate strike killed two people and left 18 others wounded. Another five people were killed in aerial bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.
Russia has also struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating.
The water supply in Kyiv was entirely cut off "due to enemy attacks and damage to the capital's energy infrastructure", the main water supplier Kyivvodokanal said. The entire metro network was suspended on Tuesday and Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult".
As Ukraine was counting its dead, the Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November.
It will be the first trilateral meeting since February. Since then, Russia and the US have begun engaging more directly, with US President Donald Trump announcing a deal to import Russian diesel.
Speaking to reporters in Berlin on Tuesday, Zelensky said that it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations on a ceasefire and a peaceful settlement, but that he had so far had not seen "any indication" of that being the case.
Several rounds of ceasefire talks late last year yielded no results, and in public declarations Russian officials have generally refused to budge from Moscow's maximalist demand of effective Ukrainian surrender.
US First Lady Melania Trump Melania Trump, who was credited with brokering a truce last week in the besieged town of Oleshky, is set to host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday. However, no details were given in the White House statement of who was due to attend the meeting. , external
The UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level", as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its advances on the front line have since stalled, and attacks on Ukraine have intensified, with Moscow employing large numbers of missiles and drones to strike Ukrainian cities.
At the same time, Ukraine is faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries of weapons and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles.
In Berlin, Zelensky acknowledged that although the front line was stable "the situation in the air was not as positive, particularly when it comes to our air defence capabilities and the protection of our civilian population".

articles.title_zh: iPhone 18 will have two upgrades inspired by ‘Pro’ models, per leak
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s iPhone 17 is already an option for buyers looking to upgrade, but the timing of the next generation could make the decision more complicated. With the iPhone 18 reportedly expected to launch in March 2027, only a few months remain before the anticipated release. This leaves potential buyers weighing whether to purchase a new iPhone now or wait for Apple’s next move.
The regular iPhone 18 is expected to arrive in spring 2027, with reports pointing to a possible March launch. Apple has yet to confirm the date, but the revised release schedule could affect buyers planning an upgrade.
Note : The article is based on the writer's opinion.
If you are planning to buy a new iPhone, the iPhone 17 remains a strong option. According to a recent leak from Digital Chat Station on Weibo , the standard iPhone 18 may not bring major changes to the overall design or camera hardware. It is expected to retain a 6.3-inch 120Hz OLED display and dual 48MP rear cameras.
However, the new model could arrive at a higher price than its predecessor. The iPhone 18 is expected to launch in March or April 2027. This means buyers may have to wait several months for a phone that could offer only incremental improvements.
While the A20 chip and a larger battery could improve performance and battery life, Apple has yet to confirm these details. Meanwhile, the iPhone 17 already offers a 120Hz ProMotion display, the A19 chip, and capable dual rear cameras. Its performance is more than enough for everyday tasks, gaming, and photography.
It also supports Apple Intelligence and offers a premium experience without requiring buyers to wait for another generation. If your current phone needs replacing, the iPhone 17 is worth considering, especially if you find it at a good discount.
Waiting for the iPhone 18 makes more sense if you prefer newer hardware and are willing to pay extra for potential improvements.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
articles.title_zh: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he hopes upcoming United States-mediated talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi will lead to a three-way meeting of leaders that includes Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking in Berlin on Tuesday alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Zelenskyy said the adviser-level talks, set for November 10 and 11 , were part of a broader diplomatic push to end the war.
“We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
Asked about the Abu Dhabi talks, Merz said it was “important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement”.
“I do not see that happening so far,” the chancellor said.
Zelenskyy’s visit to Berlin was not announced in advance for security reasons.
On landing, he said on X that diplomatic coordination, strengthening air defences and supporting Ukraine’s energy sector would top the agenda.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff announced the new round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US on Monday. He said the discussions would focus on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace”.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that a Russian delegation would attend, led as before by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported.
The build-up to next week’s talks follows one of the most notable displays of cooperation between the warring sides since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Last week, human rights ombudsmen from Russia and Ukraine oversaw a local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in a mission brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Putin and Zelenskyy have had no direct contact since the invasion, and their representatives have held only a handful of rounds of talks.
Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane, reporting from Berlin, said there was a clear sense from Zelenskyy and Merz that the Abu Dhabi meeting “is a step forward, and there was an element of positivity about it”.
He said one journalist raised an important issue, saying “Europe and Ukraine are supposedly in lockstep with each other”, before asking, “why then are the Europeans not going to be in Abu Dhabi in those talks?”
“There was not much of a reply there, but it’s clearly an issue, a thorny issue, perhaps, certainly for the Europeans,” Kane said.
European governments have insisted on being involved in the negotiations but are unlikely to be at the table in Abu Dhabi.
Instead, US envoys are due to meet representatives from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, NATO and the European Union in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe’s post-war security architecture.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs an additional 70 billion euros ($77.5bn) from European countries next year.
Kane said successive German governments had pledged their full support to Ukraine, financing its efforts to fend off Russian attacks and supplying weapons and ammunition.
But he said Merz knows that “the financial aspect of helping Ukraine has become a real issue, given that the economy here and in other European countries is particularly threatened right now”.
“The cost of living in this country for many voters has become a serious issue,” Kane said.
He added that parties opposed to funding Ukraine, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Die Linke, were “prospering in the polls and in elections”.
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin may hold three-way talks on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 and 19 .
Around the same time, the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of about 35 countries backing Ukraine, is due to meet in Berlin.
The Group of 20 (G20) summit follows in Florida from December 13 to 15 , where it remains unclear whether Putin will attend for the first time since the invasion.

articles.title_orig: Ben Saul Attempts to Whitewash $150,000 from China
articles.title_zh: Ben Saul Attempts to Whitewash $150,000 from China
articles.content_orig:
At an October 22, 2026 UN press conference , Ben Saul, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights while countering terrorism, was questioned about his ties to China. The questions followed a UN Watch report revealing that China had contributed $150,000 to his mandate in 2024, as documented in the UN’s 2024 Special Procedures Facts & Figures report , as well as allegations concerning his close personal ties to a Chinese Communist Party official.
Saul’s claims in response raise several questions which are examined below:
Rebuttal: Saul initially suggested that China’s $150,000 contribution was part of its ordinary funding of the United Nations. He emphasized that China is “the second largest contributor to the United Nations budget,” adding that “of course” it funds “United Nations mechanisms, including the human rights system.” He also described the funds as “an allocation which goes to the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in Geneva.”
However, the $150,000 did not come from China’s assessed contributions to the UN regular budget. It was a separate, voluntary contribution specifically earmarked for Saul’s mandate.
Moreover, Saul subsequently contradicted his own suggestion that China’s contribution was part of its ordinary UN funding, asserting that his “mandate and many others get no UN regular budget funding.” Not only did this undercut his earlier explanation, but the assertion itself was false. As OHCHR’s own website makes clear, Special Procedures mandates do receive support from the UN regular budget for various activities, including travel to Geneva and New York to present reports to the Human Rights Council and General Assembly, participation in annual meetings, country visits, and other mandated activities.
This regular-budget support is provided through the UN system and is not separately reported as voluntary contributions in the annual Special Procedures Facts & Figures reports .
Thus, Saul’s explanation was misleading in two respects. First, by invoking China’s status as a major contributor to the UN budget, he obscured the distinction between its mandatory contributions and its separate, earmarked funding of his mandate. Second, his categorical assertion that his mandate receives “no UN regular budget funding” ignored the regular-budget support that OHCHR itself identifies as available to Special Procedures.
Rebuttal: Saul portrayed China’s contribution as entirely routine, stating that “there is nothing unusual or untoward about that” and noting that his “mandate also gets some contributions from Spain and Switzerland.”
It is true that Special Procedures mandates rely in part on voluntary contributions from Member States. As OHCHR explains , the UN’s regular budget is insufficient to cover all mandate activities, making additional voluntary contributions necessary under the current system.
OHCHR further states that these contributions are “received by OHCHR,” are “strictly governed by UN financial rules, policies and oversight mechanisms,” and “do not give donors any role in the appointment, direction, priorities, findings or conclusions of mandate holders.” This is consistent with Saul’s assertion that the Chinese funds were channeled through OHCHR in Geneva and that China has no direct control over their expenditure.
However, the fact that voluntary contributions are permitted under UN rules does not mean that China’s contribution to Saul’s mandate was routine.
First , China is not among OHCHR’s leading voluntary contributors. In 2024, China contributed $4 million in voluntary funding, ranking 18th among donors. Yet despite its relatively modest overall contributions, China chose to earmark $150,000 specifically for Saul’s mandate.
Second , China’s contribution was earmarked for Saul’s particular mandate rather than provided as general support for the Special Procedures system. OHCHR distinguishes between earmarked and unearmarked voluntary contributions. Significantly, in Resolution 16/21 , the Human Rights Council welcomed additional voluntary contributions while expressly emphasizing that such contributions should be, to the extent possible, unearmarked.
Third , China’s earmarked funding of Special Procedures has been highly selective. According to UN Watch’s Special Procedures Funding Database , between 2017 and 2025, China contributed a total of $2,249,979 in earmarked funding to just seven of the more than 55 Special Procedures mandates.
Felipe Gonzalez Morales, 2022
The pattern of funding is noteworthy. China has directed substantial earmarked contributions to a small group of mandates, including several whose work impacts China’s domestic issues and foreign policy positions. Most notably, more than $1 million went to the Special Rapporteur on unilateral coercive measures, a mandate focused on condemning sanctions and other measures imposed by Western governments.
Ben Saul is also the only Special Rapporteur on human rights while countering terrorism identified in the database as having received earmarked funding from China.
Saul’s observation that Spain and Switzerland also contribute to his mandate does not address the central issue. China is not a leading voluntary donor to OHCHR, yet it specifically selected Saul’s mandate for a $150,000 earmarked contribution. The question is not whether China is permitted to contribute to the UN human rights system, but why it chose to fund this particular mandate rather than support the Special Procedures system generally.
Rebuttal: Saul emphatically asserted that China does not have “any control over the way that money is spent.” OHCHR similarly states that voluntary contributions are governed by “UN financial rules, policies and oversight mechanisms” that do not give donors “any role in the appointment, direction, priorities, findings or conclusions of mandate holders.”
However, the absence of formal donor control does not preclude indirect influence over a mandate-holder’s priorities and agenda.
A study published by the European Centre for Law and Justice (ECLJ), based on interviews with mandate-holders conducted between 2015 and 2019, documented concerns about the influence of voluntary funding on the work of UN human rights experts. The study quoted a former chair of the Coordination Committee of Special Procedures, who warned that donor funding could shape experts’ agendas. The report also noted that several experts described funding arrangements in which financial support was conditional upon undertaking specific projects related to their mandates (pp. 37–38).
These findings illustrate why compliance with UN financial rules does not, by itself, resolve concerns about the potential influence of earmarked funding.
Saul also asserted that China’s contribution “goes simply to funding the staff that support my mandate in Geneva and New York.” However, he provided no supporting documentation and the 2024 Facts & Figures Report does not establish how the $150,000 was ultimately spent. Even accepting his explanation, the use of the funds for staffing would not, in itself, resolve questions about the potential influence of earmarked funding on a mandate-holder’s priorities.
Rebuttal: Saul further claimed that he has “criticized China on many occasions,” citing his work on Xinjiang, Hong Kong’s National Security Law, and the prosecution of Jimmy Lai.
Yet his record is more limited than his broad assurances suggest. Saul has not dedicated a single report or country visit to China and has not issued a standalone public statement specifically addressing China’s treatment of Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang. Although his 2025 General Assembly report briefly addressed the situation in Xinjiang, it did so within a broader thematic report on administrative counterterrorism measures.

articles.content_orig:
RedMagic Android Announcement
Back in mid-October, the RedMagic 12 Pro+ was unveiled in China , and RedMagic said at the time that it would also launch globally as the RedMagic 12 Pro. Today, the RedMagic 12 Pro is official for the rest of the world, and it keeps the RGB-lit liquid cooling and the 8,400 mAh battery of its Chinese counterpart.
That battery is 12% bigger than the 7,500 mAh cell in the RedMagic 11 Pro , yet the new handset is thinner, at 8.5mm (vs. 8.9mm). Charging is where the global model differs from the Chinese one - you get 80W wired charging instead of 120W, along with wireless and bypass charging.
The 6.85-inch 1.5K BOE-made X11 OLED screen has what the company says is the industry's first 185Hz refresh rate paired with a 'true full-screen' design with an under-display selfie camera. The panel comes with 0.96mm bezels, reaches 1,900 nits of global peak brightness and 5,000 nits of local peak brightness, and offers an instantaneous touch sampling rate of up to 5,000Hz. Hidden underneath are a ninth-generation 16MP selfie camera developed with BOE and a 3D ultrasonic fingerprint reader.
The Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset is at the helm, joined by the in-house RedCore R5 gaming chip and the G1 display chip, with up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. On the back, there's a 50MP main camera with OIS and a 50MP ultrawide.
The RedMagic 12 Pro in Nightfreeze
The AquaCore Cooling System 3.0 combines the dual-loop liquid cooling, which now lights up in RGB, with a 25,500 RPM fan, a vapor chamber with a 15% larger effective cooling area, and Liquid Metal 4.0. The new micro-pump delivers up to 130kPa of output pressure, 85% more than its predecessor's, while drawing as little as 20mW.
The phone is IP68/IP69-rated for dust and water resistance, while the fan area carries a separate IPX8 rating. You also get 520Hz shoulder triggers (the Chinese model's are rated at 700Hz), stereo speakers with Dolby Atmos, an X-axis linear motor, an IR blaster, NFC, Wi-Fi 7, and a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port. It runs RedMagic OS 12 based on Android 17, with Gemini integration, PC game emulation, and Steam access through the X-Gravity gaming center.
The RedMagic 12 Pro in Subzero
The RedMagic 12 Pro comes in Nightfreeze (transparent black) and Subzero (transparent silver) color options. Here's a handy table with pricing information for all possible versions.
For comparison, the RedMagic 11 Pro started at €699 last year, so every configuration is now €200 more expensive, and the top one also drops from 24GB to 16GB of RAM.
Early Bird vouchers will be sold from November 12 to 17, and voucher holders can place orders on November 17, getting a free 80W charger and a RedMagic-branded item. Open sales start on November 18 through RedMagic's official online stores and select retailers in North America, most of the EU, the UK, parts of Asia Pacific, the Middle East, Mexico, and Chile.

articles.title_orig: Sanctions-evading China-bound billions turn untraceable in Moscow
articles.title_zh: Sanctions-evading China-bound billions turn untraceable in Moscow
articles.content_orig:
Keep independent journalism alive
At the sprawling Sadovod market in southeast Moscow, among the 160 acres of clothing, jewelry and appliance booths, at least eight teams are spotted, working apart from the everyday hustle and bustle of the market.
Throughout a business day, these teams, known in confidential records as “departments,” receive a steady stream of customers, almost always carrying bags of various shapes and sizes.
And inside the bags are piles and piles of cash – Russian rubles. These departments, staffed by payment brokers, are a key intake point for one of the largest, and most secretive, cash-processing operations in the world.
Welcome to the industrial cash machine that is A7, the payments giant backed by the Russian state.
Between November 2024 and July 2025, A7 processed at least 283 tons of cash rubles, worth more than $14 billion, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and Russian independent media outlet Proekt has found.
For A7, ICIJ discovered, cash is king, the jet fuel for a firm now under scrutiny as a “shadow banking network” designed to evade Western sanctions at scale, according to US authorities.
On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned A7 as a “significant transnational criminal organization,” which “utilizes money laundering methodologies to fraudulently move vast sums of money in violation of sanctions and other laws in the jurisdictions in which it operates.”
But while Western governments and banks scramble to trace A7 money flows through the international financial system, ICIJ’s investigation reveals that the origins of the bulk of A7 transmissions are, in fact, untraceable.
According to internal A7 records seen by ICIJ, and people familiar with the matter, a huge portion of A7’s payments do not stem from conventional bank transfers by clients inside Russia, but literally from hundreds of tons of cash rubles.
Leaked internal records allowed ICIJ to identify that a handful of wholesale markets and other businesses around the Russian capital, including Sadovod, where much of the business is done in cash, made up a significant share of the cash A7 processed.
The records show that while the source of the cash is untraceable, its destination is not: Most of the cash is bound not for Western markets, but for China.
A7 did not respond to ICIJ’s requests for comment.
In public statements, A7 has strongly rejected the US allegations of wrongdoing, saying that it “employs a modern, multi-tiered compliance system” and that it was “established to ensure uninterrupted settlements for the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures.”
“All clients undergo screening to identify risks and prevent the servicing of individuals or organizations whose activities violate regulatory requirements,” it continued.
Experts say the fact that cash drives A7 raises the specter of a money laundering operation limited only by the size of the market and A7’s capacity to physically handle the cash. As such, A7’s cash-based model presents not-previously-understood challenges both to the conventional banking system and to law enforcement.
“Cash is considered one of the highest risk methods of payment and store of value because it’s anonymous, it can travel across borders, and it doesn’t attach to any specific individual or company,” George Voloshin, an expert at ACAMS , a global training body for anti-financial crime, told ICIJ in an interview.
“The A7 network not only helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions and export controls,” Voloshin continued. The fact that A7 takes massive volumes of cash from Moscow’s wholesale markets suggests that the company “is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering by effectively legitimizing potential proceeds of crime,” he said.
Voloshin added that international banks bear an additional burden of tracing payments emanating from A7. “The main risk is that [foreign] intermediary or beneficiary banks become complicit in [a] form of criminal activity that they know nothing about, because they don’t have any visibility into what’s happening in Russia where the money originates from.”
On its launch in late 2024, A7 touted itself as a sanctions-proof payments system, and has come under increasing scrutiny for its role as one of the Kremlin’s principal channels for laundering billions of dollars worth of payments out of Russia and into the global financial system, via a global network of shell companies, often with accounts at major international banks.
As part of its launch, A7 integrated into its business a hodgepodge of informal payment brokers at Moscow markets, including Sadovod, according to internal A7 records seen by ICIJ.
For A7, “Sadovod is simply a big client base – a big, aggregated pile of clients,” a person familiar with the matter, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, told ICIJ. “And that’s exactly what they go there for: the money and the profit.”
For years, this ecosystem of market brokers converted importers’ cash into conventional bank transfers or crypto, most often bound for China. This informal system was upended by Western sanctions, which barred Russian businesses from the SWIFT system, the international messaging network that allows banks to exchange transactions. The threat of US secondary sanctions – which target entities for doing business with sanctioned states or businesses – made Chinese banks more cautious when dealing with Russia.
The informal cash payment system at Moscow’s wholesale markets “depends on trusted intermediaries, established relationships and confidence that money will arrive,” Ilia Shumanov, managing partner of Russia-focused due diligence firm Tri-Trace Investigations, told ICIJ. “Its international reach can be extensive, while outsiders have limited visibility into the underlying transactions.”
Under A7’s new, supercharged system, a platoon of market brokers takes in the bags of cash brought by vendors and makes an initial count.
The brokers then stuff the rubles into numbered bags to be loaded, along with clients’ payment orders, into vans bound for an A7 processing office elsewhere in the Russian capital, according to leaked internal payment and cash management records.
A review of cash deposit and internal payment records shows that a small army of 50 or so A7 cashiers feeds the cash into a counting system where the amounts are verified; A7 enters the bag number, ruble amount and the client’s payment order into a bespoke payment management system, then trucks the cash on to Promsvyazbank, or PSB, the Russian state defense bank, a co-owner of the company. PSB puts it in a vault and credits A7 accounts.
PSB acknowledged ICIJ’s request for comment, but did not provide a response.
Records show that A7 then orders one of a network of shell companies registered outside Russia to make a payment on behalf of an A7 client to a beneficiary’s account, often a Chinese exporter, at another bank outside Russia – without any trace of the cash, or Russian origin, of the funds surfacing on the wire transfer or supporting documentation. The shell companies are advanced funds from A7 in Russia which pass through Kyrgyzstan on their way to the payee.
“The only bank that sees [where the funds come from] is Promsvyazbank,” Voloshin commented. “And the only company that sees everything is A7 itself.”
With A7’s role in sanctions evasion increasingly in the spotlight of Western authorities, understanding the source of A7 payments will become a central challenge for Western sanctions enforcers and international banks charged with know-your-customer (KYC) and other anti-money-laundering obligations.
The scale of A7’s cash intake is visible in a series of leaked documents reviewed by ICIJ, including a cash deposit ledger dated to shortly after the company’s launch in late 2024. Over a six-week period between November and December 2024, that ledger and other documents provide a running total of

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.
I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters .
My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.
In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.
These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.
Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.
iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums , the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple :
Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos
Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.
There are a ton of other great additions in iOS 27.2, which you can read about below:
What are your favorite iOS 27.2 features so far? Let us know in the comments.
